Kryzhopil Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Vinnytsia Oblast, Ukraine

Not demolished. Kryzhopil was founded in 1866 as a railway station, and its rail connection to Odessa — documented at length elsewhere in this collection — became a genuine economic lifeline for local Jewish traders right up to WWII. The town suffered two separate pogroms in 1919, in May and August, killing 60 people combined. Under Romanian administration during WWII, the town's prayer house and the oldest part of this very cemetery were demolished, with the matzevot used to pave the town's central street; Kryzhopil also served as a transit point for Jewish deportees sent from Romania itself into Transnistria, many of whom died here and were buried in this cemetery. After the war, a small, semi-clandestine religious community persisted, maintained by both a rabbi and a shochet.
